Modal Verbs in the Passive Voice

You use modal verbs to add meaning to other verbs. They come before the dictionary form (infinitive without ‘to') of the main verb.
Modal verbs can add meaning connected with speculations, certainty or obligation.

You can use modal verbs in the passive voice.
You use the passive an voice when you want to focus on the receiver of the action, rather than the ‘doer' of the action.

Here is the structure of a passive sentence:

Subject + to be + past participle
You can add a modal verb before to be.
Subject + modal + to be + past participle
Here the sentence now has an additional meaning of possibility because of the modal may.
He would be put in jail if this practice was adopted here.
But there are standards which international companies may be expected to follow.
Very poor children could be protected from others who might lead them into illegal activities.
Are there international requirements that could be demanded of a business?
Using Expressions like “of course” and “in fact”
You use expressions like of course, in fact, naturally, believe it or not, and really to emphasize that something is true.

• To say that you agree or disagree with someone
    • Of course. But has he broken any international laws?

• To say something that you believe someone probably already knows or will not be surprised about.
    • Of course, there are justifications.

• To add something to what you have just said, especially something that may seem surprising.
    • In fact, these children start at the age of seven.
You also use phrases like "really", "naturally", " believe it or not" and "it is obvious" to emphasize that something is true.
His manufacturing really is outsourced and, believe it or not, involves child labor.
Naturally, he would be put in jail if this practice was adopted here.
In fact, these children start at the age of seven.
It is obvious that the homework, which should have been done by him, wasn't done properly.

images.text:
Paulo: Ferdinand, my investigation may be finished. I can tell you that I found the missing piece of the puzzle.
Ferdinand: What did you discover?
Paulo: His manufacturing really is outsourced and, believe it or not, involves child labor. Naturally, he would be put in jail if this practice was adopted here.
Ferdinand: Of course. But has he broken any international laws?
Paulo: As it happens, none of the foreign country's laws have been broken. But there are standards which international companies may be expected to follow. And, the fact remains that child labor is illegal in countries where the clothes would be marketed. They might be at the center of a major scandal. Of course, child labor breaks international labor standards.

Ferdinand: Are these teenagers?
Paulo: No. In fact, these children start at the age of seven. Of course, there are justifications. For instance, very poor children could be protected from others who might lead them into illegal activities.
Ferdinand: There are more humane alternatives. This should be reported immediately.
Paulo: Yes, but hold your horses. Holly's is not a social service.

Ferdinand Right. Are there international requirements that could be demanded for a business?
Paulo: They aren't powerful because countries don't all agree. Of course, there are watchdog organizations that could be used. They use social pressure.
Ferdinand: Do you think Farmani is aware of this?
Paulo: It's hard to say. Children must be hidden when foreigners come to visit the factories. But it is obvious that the homework, which should have been done by him, wasn't done properly.
